title: Semantic layers and metrics
summary: Why one definition per metric matters, the core concepts and metric types, the main implementations, and semantic layers as grounding for LLMs.

blocks.text: Ask three teams for last month's revenue and you may get three numbers: one includes tax, one excludes refunds, one uses order date instead of payment date. Each number is defined in a different dashboard, notebook or spreadsheet. A **semantic layer** fixes this by defining business concepts (entities, dimensions, metrics) once, in code, and generating the SQL for every consumer.

layers.label: Consumers
layers.sub: BI tools, notebooks, spreadsheets, apps, LLM agents

layers.label: Semantic layer
layers.sub: metrics, dimensions, entities, joins; query API

layers.label: Gold marts
layers.sub: facts and dimensions at known grain (chapter 15)

items: **Consistency**: one definition of *revenue*, versioned and reviewed like code.
**Correct joins**: the layer knows relationships and grain, so users cannot accidentally double count.
**Reuse across tools**: the same metric in a dashboard, a notebook and an API ("headless BI").
**Governance**: access rules and certification apply at the metric level.

head: Concept
Meaning
Example
rows: A business object with a key; used to join semantic models
An attribute to group or filter by; categorical or time
An aggregation over a column of a model
A business-facing definition built from measures

blocks.text: The separation between measure and metric matters: a measure is a mechanical aggregation on one table; a metric adds business meaning, filters, ratios or time windows, and can combine measures from different models through shared entities.

head: Type
Definition
Example
Trap it avoids
rows: Numerator metric / denominator metric, each aggregated first
Aggregate over a running or trailing window
7-day rolling active users; revenue to date
Expression over other metrics, including time offsets
gross margin = (revenue - cogs) / revenue; growth vs last month

blocks.text: Ratios must be computed as aggregate-then-divide at the requested grain. Averaging daily conversion rates to get a monthly rate weights small days the same as large ones and gives a wrong answer.

MetricFlow is the engine behind the dbt Semantic Layer, and has been open-sourced under the Apache 2.0 licence (check the current licence terms). You declare **semantic models** on top of dbt models and **metrics** on top of their measures; MetricFlow builds a join graph from entities and generates SQL for a query such as *revenue by customer region by month*.

blocks.title: MetricFlow semantic model and metric
blocks.text:
semantic_models:
  - name: orders
    model: ref('fct_orders')
    defaults:
      agg_time_dimension: order_date
    entities:
      - name: order
        type: primary
        expr: order_id
      - name: customer
        type: foreign
        expr: customer_id
    dimensions:
      - name: order_date
        type: time
        type_params:
          time_granularity: day
      - name: status
        type: categorical
    measures:
      - name: order_amount
        agg: sum
        expr: amount
      - name: order_count
        agg: sum
        expr: 1

metrics:
  - name: revenue
    label: Revenue
    type: simple
    type_params:
      measure: order_amount
    filter: "{{ Dimension('order__status') }} = 'paid'"

Queries go through the dbt CLI or APIs, for example `dbt sl query --metrics revenue --group-by metric_time__month` (dbt platform) or `mf query` with open-source MetricFlow. The YAML specification has been evolving (newer releases change how measures are declared), so check the current documentation for your version. Chapter 36 builds a full model.

blocks.title: Cube data model
blocks.text:
cubes:
  - name: orders
    sql_table: analytics.fct_orders
    joins:
      - name: customers
        sql: "{CUBE}.customer_id = {customers}.customer_id"
        relationship: many_to_one
    measures:
      - name: revenue
        sql: amount
        type: sum
    dimensions:
      - name: order_id
        sql: order_id
        type: number
        primary_key: true
The Open Semantic Interchange initiative aims at a vendor-neutral format for semantic definitions. Treat portability as a goal, not a given: check the current documentation of the tools you use.
"Headless" means the metric logic is separated from any one presentation tool. Dashboards, notebooks, reverse-ETL jobs and applications all call the same API. The trade-offs:

items: **Pro**: one definition, many front ends; metrics survive a BI tool migration.
**Con**: another service in the query path, with its own latency, caching and availability concerns.
**Con**: not every BI tool integrates natively; some only see a SQL endpoint or exported tables.
**Practice**: start with the 20 to 50 metrics that leadership reviews, not with every column.

blocks.text: 35.6 Semantic layers as grounding for LLMs

Text-to-SQL directly on raw schemas fails in predictable ways: wrong joins, wrong grain, invented filters, a different definition of *active customer* every time. A semantic layer gives an LLM a small, documented vocabulary of metrics and dimensions. The model chooses *which* metric and dimensions to request; the semantic engine generates the SQL deterministically.

blocks.title: Fewer wrong answers from an analytics assistant
blocks.text: A SaaS company piloted an assistant that wrote SQL against 400 gold tables. Reviewers found frequent errors in joins and churn definitions. The analytics engineering team exposed 35 certified metrics through a semantic layer and restricted the assistant to querying it.
items: Answers now cite the metric definition used.
Questions outside the model return *not available* instead of a guessed query.
Access policies are enforced because SQL runs under the user's role.

blocks.title: Define the metric catalogue
blocks.text: A subscription business argues about MRR, churn rate and net revenue retention. Draft the entities, dimensions, measures and metrics (with metric types) needed to answer these questions consistently, and decide which metrics must be ratio or cumulative.
hints: At which grain is each underlying fact stored?
Which definitions need sign-off from finance?

items: A semantic layer defines entities, dimensions, measures and metrics once and generates SQL for every consumer.
Metric types: simple, ratio, cumulative, derived; ratios aggregate first, then divide.
MetricFlow powers the dbt Semantic Layer; Cube, LookML and Snowflake semantic views are alternatives.
Headless BI separates metric logic from presentation, at the cost of another query-path service.
Semantic layers ground LLM analytics: the model picks metrics, the engine writes the SQL.

blocks.q: Conversion rate is stored per day. How should a correct monthly conversion rate be computed?
options: Sum conversions and sum visits for the month, then divide
blocks.explain: Ratio metrics aggregate numerator and denominator at the requested grain, then divide. Averaging daily rates overweights low-traffic days.

blocks.q: What role do entities play in MetricFlow?
options: They are keys that let MetricFlow join semantic models
blocks.explain: Entities (primary, foreign, unique) form the join graph so metrics from one model can be grouped by dimensions from another.

blocks.q: Why does a semantic layer improve LLM-based analytics?
options: The LLM chooses governed metrics and dimensions while SQL is generated deterministically
It trains the LLM on warehouse data
It removes the need for access control
blocks.explain: The semantic layer constrains the vocabulary and handles joins and grain. It does not train the model, and access control still applies.

blocks.q: Which is a real cost of headless BI?
options: Only one BI tool can be used
An additional service sits in the query path with latency and availability concerns
Metrics can no longer be versioned
blocks.explain: A separate semantic service adds an operational dependency. Its benefits are versioned, shared metrics across many tools.
